title: Roger Allam in How The Other Half Loves - theatre review
transcript: Hello, and welcome to Theatre Reviews with Paul seven. I'm here at the Old Vic to see Now the Other Half Loves. >> >> There was a time when there were five plays by Alan Ayckbourn running at the same time in the West End. And that was back in 1975. He's gone out of fashion since then. His work is not so regularly regularly performed these days. So, it's quite possible that there are theatre-goers who've never seen one of his plays. In which case, this is the perfect introduction. It's a farce about infidelity infused with deception and misunderstandings. A cast whose comic timing works with the precision of a Swiss watch. And uh talking of running at the same time, a set in which two sitting rooms occupy the same space and the action segues between the two. Oh, and Roger Allam's in it. Keep watching and I'll tell you more about the funniest play in London right now. Before we move on, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel. And visit my website theatre.reviews where you can read written versions of my reviews and my roundups of other critics' reviews of the major London shows. I didn't even mention that this production at the Old Vic takes place in the round as it did when the play was premiered back in 1969. Since it's nearly always performed with a proscenium arch, it's it's fascinating to see what a difference this makes. You really feel you're in the thick of it with actors entering and exiting in four different directions, front, back, and sides. And and Rob Howell's set is a masterpiece of construction. He presents two sitting rooms in the same space while keeping it simple enough not to block anyone's view. The set evokes the late '60s and early '70s with some deft touches in the choice of furniture and costumes including Roger Allam's very short shorts and two phones from that period, one traditional and one more trendy which are used for some comically misleading calls between the two houses. The households that are present on stage belong to two couples, well-off Frank and Fiona and flat-dwelling Bob and Teresa. Fiona and Bob are having a secret affair. To try and keep it that way when their partners become suspicious, they both independently pretend that they are spending time helping someone who suspects their partner is having an affair. The two someones in question are another couple, William and Mary. Things start to spiral out of control when Frank and Teresa respectively invite William and Mary to dinners on successive nights. The simultaneous view of what other characters are doing elsewhere underlines the secrets, the lies and the self-deception. The highlight of this is that the consecutive dinners take place on stage simultaneously with William and Mary flitting between the two culminating in a a hilarious incident with flying soup. Now, you may know that on my website I compile roundups of critics' reviews. Well, they all gave high praise to Roger Allam's performance as Frank. More than one referring to his masterclass in comic timing and I absolutely agree. There can be no one better at the pause and the look before pouncing with a killer line. His character is pompous, but with a dimness that doesn't live up to his image of himself as someone in charge of the situation. So, he puts two and two together and makes five with the regularity. While being so absorbed in his view of the world that he doesn't notice what's happening right in front of him. And excellent as he is, all the cast are are to be commended for their comic timing. Um as is Philip Breene for directing their propulsion through time and space so well. Dorothy Atkinson's flustered Fiona is a triumph of staring looks and tight lips. Rowan Polanski moves smarmy Bob from inconsiderate to downright nasty. You can almost see the sparks coming off Aisha and Twana's fiery Teresa. William, an abusive husband, is given a slimy obsequiousness by Adam Gillen. And Laura Elsworth as Mary is painfully shy, but so full of emotion it feels like she could explode at any moment. Although concerning three very different marriages, none of them entirely happy, but all of them somehow rubbing along, How the Other Half Loves only really looks in depth at Fiona and Frank. And we can see why she might have wanted a temporary escape from the dullness of her patronizing husband. Less fully portrayed are the other two couples. In both of their cases, the men are abusive and the women seem to forgive them relatively easily. More insights into the female characters would be needed if the play were to be written today. But as a farce, it's a great night out. I give How the Other Half Loves four stars. >> >> I hope you found this review useful or interesting, and if you did, please like, comment, and subscribe to this channel, then you'll be the first to know about my future reviews. And you can read my reviews and my roundups of other critics' reviews, including those of How the Other Half Loves, at my website theatredotreviews, and you can follow me on various social media like Instagram, Facebook, uh Threads, Mastodon, and Blue Sky.
